subChunks.title: Descriptive Statistics & Distributions
subChunks.hookHtml: Consider the following salary negotiation scenario: your employer tells you that the average salary at your company is £45,000. You're being offered £32,000. Is this fair? Before you can answer, you need to know more: is that average the mean, the median, or the mode? If the CEO earns £500,000 and twenty other staff earn £28,000, the mean will be pulled upward by that one outlier, making the 'average' deeply misleading. This is not an abstract statistical curiosity — it's the difference between understanding your situation and being manipulated by a number. Statistics are the language in which psychological findings are communicated. Without statistical literacy, you are dependent on other people's interpretations of evidence, which may or may not be accurate. This chunk builds the quantitative foundations every psychologist needs.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Levels of Measurement

Before choosing a statistic, you must understand what kind of data you have. Stevens (1946) proposed four levels of measurement, each with different mathematical properties:

Nominal   — categories with no inherent order (e.g., gender, diagnosis, nationality)
Ordinal   — ranks with unequal intervals (e.g., Likert-scale responses, finishing positions)
Interval  — equal intervals, no true zero (e.g., temperature in Celsius, IQ scores)
Ratio     — equal intervals with a true zero (e.g., reaction time, height, number of errors)

The level of measurement determines which statistics are appropriate. You should not, for example, calculate a mean for nominal data (the 'average diagnosis' is meaningless).

Measures of Central Tendency

These describe the typical or central value in a distribution:

Mean (x̄): Sum of all values divided by N. Most statistically powerful but sensitive to outliers. Use when data are normally distributed and at interval/ratio level.

Median: The middle value when all scores are ranked. Robust to outliers; appropriate for ordinal data and skewed distributions. The median household income is more informative than the mean income in a skewed distribution of wealth.

Mode: The most frequently occurring value. The only appropriate measure of central tendency for nominal data. A distribution can be bimodal (two peaks) or multimodal.

Measures of Dispersion

Dispersion describes how spread out the data are:

Range: Maximum − Minimum. Simple but sensitive to extreme values.

Interquartile range (IQR): Q3 − Q1 (the spread of the middle 50% of data). More robust than range.

Variance (σ²): The average squared deviation from the mean. Squaring ensures deviations don't cancel out.

Standard deviation (σ): The square root of variance, expressed in the same units as the original data. The most interpretable measure of spread for interval/ratio data. A standard deviation of 10 on an IQ test (mean = 100) means most people score between 90 and 110.

The Normal Distribution

Many psychological variables (IQ, height, reaction time) are approximately normally distributed: a symmetrical, bell-shaped curve where the mean, median, and mode coincide. Key properties:

68% of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean
95% of scores fall within ±1.96 SDs of the mean
99.7% of scores fall within ±3 SDs of the mean

This is the basis of parametric statistics, which assume (among other things) that the data are normally distributed. When this assumption is violated (skewed distributions, outliers), non-parametric statistics are preferred.

Skewness and Kurtosis

Positive skew: The tail extends to the right; the mean is pulled above the median (e.g., reaction time distributions — most responses are fast, but occasional slow responses pull the mean up). Negative skew: The tail extends to the left; the mean is pulled below the median (e.g., exam scores where most students do well).

Kurtosis describes the 'peakedness' of a distribution. A leptokurtic distribution has heavy tails (more extreme values than a normal distribution); a platykurtic distribution is flatter with thinner tails.

Standardisation and z-Scores

A z-score expresses a raw score as a number of standard deviations above or below the mean: z = (X − μ) / σ. This allows comparison of scores from different scales. If a person scores 130 on an IQ test (mean = 100, SD = 15), their z-score is (130−100)/15 = 2.0 — they are two standard deviations above the mean, placing them in approximately the top 2.3% of the population.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen projects a histogram of exam scores from last year's cohort — a roughly bell-shaped curve, with the bulk of scores between 55 and 75.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Why does this shape matter? Because if your data look like this — symmetric, bell-shaped — you can use a whole toolkit of powerful statistical tests that assume a normal distribution. If your data look like a cliff edge skewed to one side, you need different tools. Statistics are not one-size-fits-all.

storyBeats.speaker: Real-world application
storyBeats.text: IQ is defined to have a mean of 100 and standard deviation of 15 — by design. This means roughly 68% of the population scores between 85 and 115, and 95% between 70 and 130. The diagnostic threshold for intellectual disability (IQ ≤ 70) is exactly two standard deviations below the mean. This is not an arbitrary cutoff — it emerged from the statistical properties of the distribution.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Every time you hear someone report 'the average' in the media, ask yourself: mean, median, or mode? And then ask: what does the distribution look like? The average number of legs on a human being is just under two — because a small number of amputees shift the mean below the mode of exactly two. The average is technically correct and completely useless.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A researcher measures anxiety scores (ranging from 0–60) in a sample of 10 participants before a therapy programme:

Scores: 12, 15, 18, 20, 22, 25, 28, 30, 35, 58

  1. Calculate the mean, median, and mode for this dataset. Show your working.
  2. Which measure of central tendency best represents the 'typical' anxiety level in this sample? Justify your answer.
  3. Without calculation, would you expect the standard deviation to be relatively large or small given this dataset? Explain why.
  4. The score of 58 is a potential outlier. Describe one way the researcher could investigate whether this score is genuine data or a recording error.
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. Mean: (12+15+18+20+22+25+28+30+35+58) / 10 = 263/10 = 26.3. To find the Median with 10 values, average the 5th and 6th: (22+25)/2 = 23.5. Mode: No value appears more than once in this dataset, so there is no mode.

2. The median (23.5) best represents the typical anxiety level. The score of 58 is an outlier that pulls the mean upward to 26.3 — a value higher than 8 out of 10 participants' actual scores. The median is resistant to outliers and gives a better indication of where the central mass of the data sits.

3. The standard deviation would be relatively large. The outlier score of 58 is far from the mean of 26.3 (a deviation of 31.7), and this large squared deviation will substantially inflate the variance and therefore the standard deviation. Most scores are clustered between 12 and 35, but the single extreme value forces the SD upward.

4. The researcher could: (a) return to the original data recording sheet or raw questionnaire to verify the score of 58 was correctly transcribed; (b) contact or re-interview the participant to confirm their response; (c) check whether the questionnaire allows a maximum of 60 (confirming 58 is within the possible range, not a data entry error); (d) run the analysis both with and without this outlier and report both results transparently, noting that the outlier substantially affects the mean.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
A clinical psychologist is comparing depression scores (on a 0–63 point scale, where higher = more severe) before and after a 12-week therapy programme. In the treatment group (n=20), pre-therapy scores are: mean=42, SD=8. Post-therapy scores are: mean=28, SD=9. In the control group (n=20), pre-therapy scores are: mean=41, SD=7. Post-therapy scores are: mean=40, SD=8.

Without conducting formal statistical tests, use descriptive statistics and your understanding of the normal distribution to evaluate whether the therapy appears to have been effective. What pattern in the data supports (or undermines) a conclusion of effectiveness? What further information would you want before drawing firm conclusions? Aim for 150–200 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
The descriptive statistics suggest the therapy had a meaningful effect. The treatment group's mean depression score dropped by 14 points (from 42 to 28), while the control group's mean barely changed (41 to 40 — a 1-point change). A 14-point reduction represents roughly 22% of the scale range, which appears clinically meaningful.

The standard deviations (8–9) are similar across groups and time points, suggesting comparable variability. The control group's near-stability over 12 weeks suggests that natural remission alone does not account for the treatment group's improvement.

However, several cautions apply. Without knowing the distribution shape, we cannot be confident that means are the most appropriate summary. If scores are skewed (e.g., floor effects — many participants improving to near-zero), medians might be more informative. The SD of 9 post-treatment means some participants had post-therapy scores as high as 46 (mean + 2SD), suggesting the therapy did not help everyone. I would also want to know how participants were allocated (random?), whether there was attrition, and whether the scale has established clinical significance thresholds — a 14-point reduction might or might not exceed the minimally clinically important difference.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a 16-year-old what a standard deviation is and why it matters, using a concrete example involving something they care about — perhaps sports scores, video game leaderboards, or exam marks. Make sure to explain why just knowing the average isn't enough.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: Parametric tests (e.g., t-test, ANOVA) assume interval/ratio data and a normally distributed population. Non-parametric tests (e.g., Mann-Whitney U, Wilcoxon) make fewer assumptions and are used with ordinal data or non-normal distributions.
A common survey response format (e.g., 'Strongly agree' to 'Strongly disagree'). Technically ordinal, but often analysed as interval — a controversial practice in statistics.
A standardised score expressing how many standard deviations a value is above or below the mean of its distribution. Allows comparison across different scales.
When a measure is so easy or hard that many participants score at the minimum (floor) or maximum (ceiling), restricting the range of scores and potentially obscuring real differences.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher measures the number of times participants check their phone per hour. The data are: 2, 3, 3, 4, 5, 47. Which measure of central tendency should she report, and why?
options: Mean, because it uses all the data values
Median, because it is robust to the outlier score of 47
Mode, because 3 is the most frequent value
Range, because it captures the full spread of the data
questions.correctAnswer: Median, because it is robust to the outlier score of 47
questions.explanationHtml: The score of 47 is a clear outlier that would substantially inflate the mean: (2+3+3+4+5+47)/6 = 10.7 — much higher than 5 out of 6 participants' actual scores. The median (average of 3rd and 4th values = (3+4)/2 = 3.5) is not affected by the extreme value and gives a better representation of the typical frequency. The mode (3) is also an option, but the median is generally preferred for skewed continuous data. Range is a measure of dispersion, not central tendency.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: In a perfectly normal distribution, approximately 95% of scores fall within one standard deviation of the mean.
questions.explanationHtml: This is false. In a normal distribution, approximately 68% of scores fall within ±1 SD of the mean, not 95%. Approximately 95% of scores fall within ±1.96 SDs of the mean (often approximated as 2 SDs). This 95% interval is the basis of confidence intervals and the conventional p < .05 threshold in hypothesis testing.

questions.questionHtml: A psychologist asks 200 participants to rate their job satisfaction on a 5-point scale (1 = very unsatisfied, 5 = very satisfied). What is the appropriate level of measurement for this data, and what measure of central tendency should be reported?
questions.explanationHtml: A 5-point rating scale is ordinal: responses have a meaningful order (5 > 4 > 3 > 2 > 1), but the intervals between points are not necessarily equal (the difference in satisfaction between 1 and 2 may not be the same as between 4 and 5). For ordinal data, the mean is technically inappropriate (though often used in practice), and the median or mode is preferred. It is not interval/ratio data because there is no true equal-interval measurement — we assume, rather than demonstrate, interval properties.

subChunks.title: Inferential Statistics & Choosing Tests
subChunks.hookHtml: Suppose you develop a new technique for improving working memory in children with ADHD and test it on 30 children, finding that the treatment group performs better on average. How confident should you be that this improvement is real — that it reflects a genuine effect of your intervention, not just random variation in how children happened to perform on that particular day? Inferential statistics exist precisely to answer this question. They allow you to move from the particular (your sample of 30) to the general (conclusions about all children with ADHD) — but only under specific conditions, and with explicitly quantified uncertainty. Understanding which statistical test to use, and what the results mean, is not optional background knowledge for a psychologist. It is the difference between producing evidence and producing noise.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The Logic of Hypothesis Testing

Inferential statistics operate via null hypothesis significance testing (NHST):

H₀ (null hypothesis):      No effect; any observed difference is due to chance
H₁ (alternative hypothesis): There is a real effect

We collect data, compute a test statistic, and determine the probability
of obtaining that statistic (or more extreme) if H₀ is true.

If p ≤ .05:  We reject H₀ — the result is 'statistically significant'
If p > .05:  We fail to reject H₀ — insufficient evidence of an effect

Critical caution: 'failing to reject H₀' does not prove H₀. Absence of evidence is not evidence of absence. A study with a small sample may simply lack the power to detect a real but small effect.

Statistical Power

Power is the probability that a study will detect a real effect if one exists. Power is influenced by:

Sample size (N)    — larger N → more power
Effect size        — larger effects are easier to detect
Alpha (α)          — lower threshold → less power
Measurement quality— reliable measures → more power

Cohen (1988) recommended aiming for 80% power as a minimum. Many classic psychology studies were severely underpowered, which partly explains why they fail to replicate.

Choosing the Right Test

Test selection depends on: (1) the research question; (2) the number of groups/conditions; (3) whether the same or different participants are in each condition; (4) the level of measurement of the DV.

Comparing two groups (independent samples, interval DV):
  → Independent samples t-test (parametric)
  → Mann-Whitney U (non-parametric)

Comparing two conditions (same participants, interval DV):
  → Paired samples t-test (parametric)
  → Wilcoxon signed-rank test (non-parametric)

Comparing three or more groups (interval DV):
  → One-way ANOVA (parametric)
  → Kruskal-Wallis (non-parametric)

Relationship between two variables (interval DV):
  → Pearson's r (parametric)
  → Spearman's rho (non-parametric)

Categorical data (frequencies):
  → Chi-squared test

Confidence Intervals

A 95% confidence interval (CI) is a range of values that, if we repeated the study many times, would contain the true population parameter 95% of the time. For example: 'The mean improvement in working memory was 4.2 points [95% CI: 1.8–6.6]' means the true population mean improvement is likely between 1.8 and 6.6 points. Crucially, if the 95% CI for a difference does not include zero, the difference is statistically significant at p < .05 — CIs and p-values contain equivalent information but CIs are more informative (they give the magnitude and direction of the effect, not just its significance).

Type I and Type II Errors

                  Reality: H₀ true    Reality: H₀ false
Decision: Reject H₀   Type I Error (α)    Correct (Power)
Decision: Retain H₀   Correct             Type II Error (β)

There is an inherent trade-off: making your significance threshold more stringent (lower α, e.g., .01 instead of .05) reduces Type I errors but increases Type II errors. The Bonferroni correction divides α by the number of tests conducted when making multiple comparisons, controlling the family-wise error rate.

Correlation and Regression

Pearson's r measures the strength and direction of the linear relationship between two interval/ratio variables. It ranges from −1 to +1. r² (coefficient of determination) is more useful: it tells you the proportion of variance in Y explained by X. r = 0.5 means r² = 0.25 — X explains 25% of the variance in Y, which is a meaningful but not overwhelming relationship.

Linear regression extends this to make predictions: given a person's score on X, what is the predicted score on Y? Multiple regression includes several predictor variables simultaneously, allowing control for confounds and assessment of each variable's unique contribution.

storyBeats.text: Dr. Chen draws a decision tree on the board, branching at questions like 'Same or different participants?' and 'Parametric or non-parametric?' A student looks overwhelmed.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: I know this looks like a lot. But notice what all these tests have in common: they all ask the same underlying question — 'could this result have occurred by chance if there were really no effect?' The tests differ in how they calculate the probability, based on the type of data. The logic is always the same.

storyBeats.speaker: Choosing a test
storyBeats.text: A researcher compares reaction times (interval data) between two independent groups — people who had coffee and people who hadn't. Same participants? No. Interval data? Yes. Normal distribution assumed? Let's check... yes. Answer: independent samples t-test. If the reaction times were severely skewed, they'd use Mann-Whitney U instead. The decision is structured, not arbitrary.

storyBeats.speaker: Dr. Miriam Chen
storyBeats.text: Confidence intervals are, in my opinion, more useful than p-values for clinical work. A p-value tells you 'probably not chance.' A confidence interval tells you 'probably between this and that' — which is the kind of information you need to make a clinical decision. Both are valuable; they're telling you different things.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
A researcher investigates whether mindfulness meditation reduces exam anxiety. She recruits 40 students and randomly assigns 20 to a mindfulness group (who complete a 4-week programme) and 20 to a control group (who continue as normal). Before and after the programme, all students complete an anxiety questionnaire (interval-level data, normally distributed).

  1. What statistical test should the researcher use to compare post-programme anxiety scores between the two groups? Explain your choice.
  2. The researcher finds t(38) = 2.41, p = .021, d = 0.76. Interpret each of these three statistics in plain language.
  3. The 95% CI for the difference in mean anxiety scores between groups is [2.1, 14.3]. What does this tell you?
  4. What is the probability of making a Type I error in this study, and what would this mean in practical terms?
subChunks.guidedPracticeModelAnswer:
1. The researcher should use an independent samples t-test (assuming the data meet parametric assumptions: approximately normal distribution, interval-level DV, independent groups). She has two independent groups (different participants in each condition), an interval-level DV (anxiety questionnaire scores), and the data are described as normally distributed. If the normality assumption were violated, she would use the Mann-Whitney U test instead.

2. t(38) = 2.41: The test statistic from the t-test with 38 degrees of freedom is 2.41. This is the ratio of the group difference to the variability within groups. p = .021: The probability of obtaining a group difference this large or larger, if there were truly no effect of mindfulness, is 2.1%. Since this is below the conventional threshold of 5%, we reject the null hypothesis. d = 0.76: Cohen's d indicates a medium-to-large effect size — the two groups differ by 0.76 standard deviations on average. This gives us information about the magnitude of the effect that p alone cannot provide.

3. The 95% CI [2.1, 14.3] tells us that we are 95% confident that the true population difference in anxiety scores between the mindfulness and control groups lies between 2.1 and 14.3 points. Since this interval does not include zero, the difference is statistically significant. The interval also tells us the minimum likely benefit (about 2 points) and the maximum (about 14 points), which is more informative for clinical decision-making than a p-value alone.

4. The probability of a Type I error is 5% (alpha = .05 by convention). In practical terms, this means that if we were to run this study 100 times when mindfulness truly had no effect, we would expect to incorrectly conclude that it does work approximately 5 times — a false positive. In this specific study, a Type I error would mean concluding that mindfulness reduces anxiety when it actually does not, potentially leading to the recommendation of an ineffective intervention.
subChunks.soloPracticeHtml:
A developmental psychologist wants to know whether there is a relationship between the number of hours per week a child spends reading (continuous, approximately normal) and their vocabulary test score (continuous, approximately normal). She collects data from 85 children and runs a Pearson correlation, obtaining r = 0.52, p < .001.

Interpret this finding fully: what does r = 0.52 tell you about the relationship? What does r² tell you? What conclusions can and cannot be drawn from this result? What alternative research design would be needed to draw stronger conclusions? Aim for 150–200 words.
subChunks.modelAnswer:
r = 0.52 indicates a moderate positive correlation between hours of reading per week and vocabulary scores — children who read more tend to have higher vocabulary scores. The relationship is positive (more reading associated with higher vocabulary) and moderate in strength, falling between Cohen's (1988) thresholds for medium (r = 0.3) and large (r = 0.5) effects.

r² = 0.52² = 0.27, meaning that hours spent reading explains approximately 27% of the variance in vocabulary scores. This is a meaningful proportion, but 73% of vocabulary variance is explained by factors other than reading time — suggesting reading is an important but far from sole contributor.

The key limitation is that causation cannot be inferred from correlation alone. Children with higher vocabulary may choose to read more (reverse causation), or a third variable — parental education, socioeconomic status, or general ability — may explain both reading habits and vocabulary. The p < .001 tells us the relationship is highly unlikely to be a chance finding given this sample size, but it does not address direction of causation.

A stronger design would be a longitudinal experiment randomly assigning children to reading programmes of different intensities, measuring vocabulary before and after. This would allow causal conclusions while controlling for pre-existing differences.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Imagine you've tested a new brain training game on 50 children and found that they scored 5 points higher on a memory test than children who didn't play the game. Explain to your 16-year-old cousin why you can't just say 'the game definitely works' — walk them through what statistical testing actually checks and why effect size matters.

rabbitHoleTerms.description: The probability of correctly detecting a real effect — i.e., rejecting H₀ when it is false. Influenced by sample size, effect size, and alpha level. Low power (< 80%) means a study may miss real effects.

A range of plausible values for a population parameter. A 95% CI will contain the true population value 95% of the time if the study is repeated under identical conditions. More informative than p-values for clinical decisions.
A statistical adjustment that divides the alpha threshold by the number of comparisons made, reducing the risk of Type I errors when multiple tests are conducted simultaneously.

The tendency for extreme measurements to move closer to the population mean on subsequent measurements — simply due to random variation. Particularly relevant in clinical research where extremely ill patients are often selected for trials.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher measures depression scores in the same 30 participants before and after a therapy programme (interval data, approximately normal). Which statistical test should she use to determine if the therapy was effective?
questions.explanationHtml: The paired samples t-test (also called the repeated-measures or dependent samples t-test) is appropriate when the same participants provide data in both conditions — which is the case here (before and after therapy). An independent samples t-test is used when different participants are in each group. Since the data are interval and approximately normal, a parametric test is appropriate; if normality were violated, the Wilcoxon signed-rank test would be the non-parametric alternative. Pearson correlation measures relationships between variables, not differences.

questions.questionHtml: True or False: A Type II error occurs when a researcher concludes there is an effect when there actually is none.
questions.explanationHtml: This describes a Type I error (false positive) — concluding there is an effect when H₀ is actually true. A Type II error is the opposite: failing to detect a real effect — concluding there is no effect when H₀ is actually false. Type II errors are associated with low statistical power and small sample sizes.

questions.questionHtml: A researcher reports r = 0.3, p = .001 for the relationship between sleep hours and cognitive performance. Which interpretation is most accurate?
options: Longer sleep explains 9% of the variance in cognitive performance, and this relationship is unlikely to be due to chance
Longer sleep explains 30% of the variance in cognitive performance
The relationship is too weak to be meaningful
questions.correctAnswer: Longer sleep explains 9% of the variance in cognitive performance, and this relationship is unlikely to be due to chance
questions.explanationHtml: r = 0.3 is a moderate positive correlation. r² = 0.3² = 0.09, meaning sleep hours explains 9% of the variance in cognitive performance — not 30% (that would be r, not r²). p = .001 tells us the result is highly unlikely to be due to chance, not that the relationship is strong. We cannot conclude causation from a correlational study alone. A 9% variance explained is modest but potentially practically important, depending on context — dismissing it as 'meaningless' is not justified.
